brief.summary: A shared, volunteer-curated catalog of free AI tools and tested prompt recipes that a small nonprofit digital-literacy group uses to help older adults with everyday tasks during drop-in sessions at public libraries.
brief.user: Bernard Kwiatkowski, 67, a retired high school chemistry teacher who volunteers two afternoons a week with TechBuddies, a digital-literacy nonprofit with one part-time paid coordinator and about 30 volunteers. He is moderately confident with AI tools and careful about privacy.
brief.moment: It's 2:15 pm at the Elm Street branch library. Mrs. Fernanda Lopes, 79, has just sat down with two needs. A letter in Portuguese from her pension office has arrived that she wants translated and explained, and a text message claims to be from her bank and wants her to 'verify' her account. Bernard has about 30 minutes with her. He wants to find what the volunteer group has already vetted for translating sensitive official letters without uploading personal ID numbers, and for checking suspected scam texts. He wants options that work on her own Android phone, so she can repeat it at home, and he would like to see what other volunteers have recommended for similar visits.
brief.data: The catalog holds 142 AI tools and 386 prompt recipes. Each tool has a cost (free, free tier with limits, paid), whether an account is needed, supported languages, device compatibility, a privacy rating from the volunteer review team (A–D), a last-tested date, and the volunteer who tested it. Each recipe has a task category (translation, scam check, letter writing, medical instructions, forms), a reading level, step count, required tool, and a redaction reminder where relevant. Volunteers have logged 1,204 session notes over 18 months, such as 'Translated Medicare letter for Cantonese speaker, worked well with recipe T-14'. Portuguese is supported by 23 tools, 9 of them rated A or B for privacy. There are 11 scam-check recipes, one flagged 'outdated, retest' since 3 Oct. Recipes are tagged by which of the group's 4 library branches use them most.

prompt:
I need the front end for Helping Hands AI Shelf. A shared, volunteer-curated catalog of free AI tools and tested prompt recipes that a small nonprofit digital-literacy group uses to help older adults with everyday tasks during drop-in sessions at public libraries.

Who's using it: Bernard Kwiatkowski, 67, a retired high school chemistry teacher who volunteers two afternoons a week with TechBuddies, a digital-literacy nonprofit with one part-time paid coordinator and about 30 volunteers. He is moderately confident with AI tools and careful about privacy.

What they're doing right now: It's 2:15 pm at the Elm Street branch library. Mrs. Fernanda Lopes, 79, has just sat down with two needs. A letter in Portuguese from her pension office has arrived that she wants translated and explained, and a text message claims to be from her bank and wants her to 'verify' her account. Bernard has about 30 minutes with her. He wants to find what the volunteer group has already vetted for translating sensitive official letters without uploading personal ID numbers, and for checking suspected scam texts. He wants options that work on her own Android phone, so she can repeat it at home, and he would like to see what other volunteers have recommended for similar visits.

What's in the system at this point: The catalog holds 142 AI tools and 386 prompt recipes. Each tool has a cost (free, free tier with limits, paid), whether an account is needed, supported languages, device compatibility, a privacy rating from the volunteer review team (A–D), a last-tested date, and the volunteer who tested it. Each recipe has a task category (translation, scam check, letter writing, medical instructions, forms), a reading level, step count, required tool, and a redaction reminder where relevant. Volunteers have logged 1,204 session notes over 18 months, such as 'Translated Medicare letter for Cantonese speaker, worked well with recipe T-14'. Portuguese is supported by 23 tools, 9 of them rated A or B for privacy. There are 11 scam-check recipes, one flagged 'outdated, retest' since 3 Oct. Recipes are tagged by which of the group's 4 library branches use them most.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
